title: Lehman and Merrill Lynch
description: http://investing.meetup.com/21 - New York Investing meetup organizer Daryl Montgomery discusses the lead up and disappearance of Lehman and Merrill Lynch as part of the special series, "Banks and Brokers Most Likely to Fail". You can also read about this subject in our blog, "The Helicopter Economics Investing Guide" at: http://nyinvesting.blogspot.com.

asr.full_text: Hello world! listed in two parts, large banks and brokers, and small and medium sized banks. Lehman as of yesterday these figures are not updated. Today it was 91%. It would have been even lower today. It actually may be number one, or exceeded Washington Mutual and you see I have an asterisk. Bear Stearns failed the day after its stock was down more than 80%. And that weekend it was gone. And the only thing that kept Lehman up, even though it was down more than 98 percent is the Fed created something called a Primary Dealer Credit Facility, in March, when Bear failed. And Lehman has barred heavily from that, and that has kept it afloat. Otherwise it would have gone under ... probably days after Bear's turn, if not the next day. And it's only a matter of time until Lehman goes under. We'll see more details later. It could even be this week, next week. Merrill Lynch 78%, serious, serious trouble too. You hit that 80 or greater percent, you should worry. The two largest brokers in trouble, Lehman down 91%. Based on today, that sounds like it's over 93%. There's no way this the market is telling you this company is dead. They lost $5.19 per share in the second quarter analyst or had it some estimate around a dollar or something, so they off about four dollars or so Was 562 this morning animals also Expected something like two dollars or less So, you know not to massive losses and the analysts like miss both of them way way both below a expectations in both The Korean Development Fund was supposed to be buying part of Lehman. I never believed this for one second. If you've read between the lines in the news analysis it was like the government didn't approve of this and this fund-is-owned by the government. So it seemed to be whoever was running it was doing this on his own accord. And then helped juice up Lehman stock. the government, so seemed to be whoever was running it was doing this on his own accord. And it helped juice up Lehman stock. Anyone knowing this could have bought Coles, made a lot of quick money, and I suspect some people did. So that fell apart yesterday, this is supposed to save Lehman. And once that fell apart, the companies finished. And then no one would buy this company, no one. And, you know, they're gonna sell, they announced there they're going to sell lots of assets. Neuberger Berman is probably worth something, they want to sell part of it, they have other assets. I mean, basically, you won't have any company left if they sell these assets. So, the company can disappear by, you know, going with the stock going to zero, or it can sell everything worth anything and the rest is worth zeros. There's many paths to oblivion. So, Merrill Lynch is slightly better off than Lehman. but not much. It raised capital as far as I can tell. And this means in stock bond type sales. December 2007. January, April and July 2008 there were at least four such incidents. It sold assets, this is not part of this capital raising above in Bloomberg and that something that was worth it and it actually worth something. They can get rid of it. They had the earnings and then they had a week later, Oh we'reibillion dollar write-offs, and they already had lost billions, so if you add those extra billion dollar write-offs, it's not clear what the lost is, because we get some tax benefit from it. So a massive, massive loss from the second quarter – they sold CDO bonds $0.05 on the dollar. It was announced that they sold it for $0.22, this is not true. If you go and actually read the specification of that sale, which sometimes you get access to, sometimes not, they loaned 75% of the money to the people who bought this. And the recourse they have if they don't pay the loan they can take back those CDOs. So if they become worthless they say we're not paying this loan. Okay give me those worthless CDOs. on the downward.

It discusses stock declines, losses, asset sales, and possible corporate failure without making a concrete investment offer, requiring payment, or requesting personal information. The meetup link is presented as a location for presentation notes, with no described connection to a deceptive offer or required financial participation.
